documents: Harmon, Laske, Crawford & Rychert 2022, Seismica 1(1), published paper (PDF, 13 pages)

entry.evidence: 70% of Earth’s surface is covered by the oceans, hampering our ability to observe variations in local mode frequencies

sequences.source_document: Harmon et al. 2022, Seismica, published paper

steps.action: Frame the gap in global normal-mode coverage over the oceans and ask whether ocean bottom seismometers can fill it.
steps.quote: Therefore, further progress in station coverage requires the deployment of ocean bottom seismometers (OBS).

steps.action: Review earlier OBS normal-mode observations (Bécel et al. 2011, Deen et al. 2017, Laske 2021), including their lowest observed modes and their noise problems.
steps.quote: Several studies reported observations of spheroidal normal modes on vertical components of very broadband OBS

steps.action: Identify tilt and compliance noise as the obstacle to low-frequency mode observation on OBS.
steps.quote: corrections to the data often need to be applied to account for tilt and compliance noise

steps.action: Select two Mw 7.9 Papua New Guinea earthquakes (2016, 2017) recorded on 15 usable T-240 broadband OBSs of the PI-LAB array.
steps.quote: The time series are from two Mw=7.9 earthquakes located in Papua New Guinea

steps.action: Build the correction chain: comb-filter deglitching of IPGP records, a new rotational tilt correction (azimuthal and vertical-radial rotation minimizing vertical RMS on a quiet day), and a DPG compliance correction.
steps.quote: We then apply a vertical – radial component rotation to minimize the energy on the rotated vertical component.

steps.action: Check the static-tilt premise by estimating tilt independently for the two events and showing consistent angles per instrument (Tables 1, 2).
steps.quote: the resulting tilt corrections are typically consistent through time for each instrument (Tables 1, 2)

steps.action: Design the evaluation: single-Slepian-taper spectra over a fixed window, with fully corrected spectra compared against uncorrected spectra.
steps.quote: We compare the spectra of the resulting data

steps.action: Set up interactive least-squares fitting of decaying cosines to estimate peak frequencies for modes 0S9–0S40 under asymptotic peak-shift theory.
steps.quote: we fit a decaying cosine function to the corresponding spectral peak in a least-squares fitting process

steps.action: Compare corrected and uncorrected time series and spectra (Figs 2–4): glitches and transients are reduced, phase amplitudes change little, and the S17D noise floor drops sharply below 2.75 mHz.
steps.quote: The corrected spectra have a much lower noise background in general, particularly below 2.75 mHz

steps.action: Compare the rotational correction with the spectral transfer-function tilt correction of Bell et al. at S17D and at lower-tilt stations (Figs S1, S2).
steps.quote: the spectral method performs worse at reducing noise at < 1 mHz

steps.action: Compile corrected spectra for all usable stations for the 2016 event (Fig. 5); find consistent fundamental spheroidal peaks, with the lowest mode 0S4 at S29D.
steps.quote: The records show very consistent peaks for the zero order spheroidal modes

steps.action: Repeat the compilation on the independent 2017 event (Fig. 6); peaks are consistent above 0S14 and 0S5 is seen at several stations.
steps.quote: for the 2017 event peaks are consistently observed above

steps.action: Compare the observed amplitude beating pattern with epicentral distance against normal-mode theory's predicted behavior.
steps.quote: This is the predicted behavior of the amplitudes of the zero order spherical harmonics

steps.action: Measure peak shifts of 0S14 and 0S23 at all stations (Fig. 7), revealing a complex spatial pattern.
steps.quote: We observe a surprisingly complex pattern of frequency shifts across the network

steps.action: Hypothesize that long-wavelength 3-D mantle structure causes the spatial variation in peak shifts.
steps.quote: hypothesize based on modelling work that long-wavelength 3-D structure can cause such variations

steps.action: Compute predicted peak shifts from S20RTS structure coefficients up to harmonic degree 12.
steps.quote: we compute normal mode structure coefficients

steps.action: Compare predicted and observed peak-shift patterns for 0S14 and 0S23.
steps.quote: exhibit similarities with our observed peak shifts

steps.action: Estimate array-averaged mode frequency shifts relative to Masters and Widmer (1995), omitting modes coupled to toroidal modes (Fig. 8).
steps.quote: we can still assess overall average mode frequency observations across the array

steps.action: Repeat the measurements on raw and on corrected records; the averages do not change significantly, and the scatter is smaller for l < 20.
steps.quote: We find that the correction does not change overall averages to a significant level.

steps.action: Compare deglitching success and lowest observed modes with previous OBS studies (Deen et al. 2017; Bécel et al. 2011; Laske 2021).
steps.quote: Our findings are similar to previous work (Deen et al., 2017)

steps.action: Retain the rotational tilt correction as an effective, energy-conserving alternative that reduces the noise floor by 2–3 orders of magnitude below about 3 mHz, while reporting that it fails on horizontal components.
steps.quote: The simple rotation to correct for tilt presented here offers an effective alternative to the commonly used spectral tilt correction

steps.action: Compare glitch handling with Bécel et al. (2011) and the high low-frequency noise floors of earlier deployments, attributing the latter to tilt.
steps.quote: This tilt noise likely exists in data from other previous experiments.

steps.action: Compare the measured shifts with 1-D reference frequencies and find deviations growing with angular order, attributed to upper-mantle heterogeneity.
steps.quote: we find deviations that increase with increasing angular order l

steps.action: Compute station-averaged S20RTS predictions of peak shifts (Fig. 9).
steps.quote: The predictions for 3-D global velocity model S20RTS are shown in Figure 9

steps.action: Compare the observations with the S20RTS predictions and find a DC offset of about 5 µHz.
steps.quote: indicates a discrepancy of a DC shift of ~5 µHz

steps.action: Revise the auxiliary of the prediction by adding the hydrostatic ellipticity correction, rather than rejecting the measurements.
steps.quote: The discrepancy can be explained by the need to account for hydrostatic ellipticity in the [...] .

steps.action: Check the 1-D reference by comparing PREM with the Masters and Widmer reference frequencies; deviations are small.
steps.quote: find relatively small deviations

steps.action: Compare the averaged observations with S20RTS+ell and SB4L18+ell predictions across angular orders (Fig. 10).
steps.quote: Our results compare favorably with two global models

steps.action: Restrict the reliable range to about 14 ≤ l ≤ 37, judging the l ≤ 14 and l > 37 results not representative of Earth structure.
steps.quote: suggesting that our result does not represent real Earth structure

steps.action: Keep the claim that the OBS frequency shifts carry real Earth-structure information, with small but significant departures from the models at 21 ≤ l ≤ 32.
steps.quote: incorporating information from OBS arrays such as ours into global normal mode inversions might improve our knowledge of Earth structure

tree.answer: Fundamental spheroidal normal modes recorded on ocean-bottom seismometers (an already known phenomenon)
Spectral peaks are observed directly after correction; peak frequencies are inferred by fitting
Characterize a rotational tilt correction and measure mode frequency shifts
For the method, the rival is the spectral transfer-function correction; for the shifts, the 3-D models S20RTS and SB4L18 (with and without ellipticity)
The two models' predictions diverge at 21 ≤ l ≤ 37; predictions with and without ellipticity differ by a DC offset
Conditions found: two natural Mw 7.9 earthquakes recorded live

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats the test with two events recorded at 15 stations
Tilt estimates agree between events; the method beats the spectral correction below 1 mHz; averages are robust to correcting the records
Correction lowers the low-frequency noise floor; shifts agree with the 3-D models for 14 ≤ l ≤ 37

end.claim: A simple rotational tilt correction lowers the low-frequency noise floor of broadband OBS vertical records, letting some stations observe spheroidal modes down to 0S4 and yielding frequency shifts that agree with 3-D models for 0S14–0S37.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the rotational tilt correction, the low-frequency noise floor would hide the modes below 2.75 mHz at tilted stations, and neither the capability claim nor the extended mode measurements would exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the data came from the PI-LAB/EURO-LAB array, designed to image the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary, not to test a normal-mode hypothesis (p. 2). Claim: the correction was tested against uncorrected data and against the spectral method, and could have failed; it did fail on horizontal components (p. 8–9). The frequency-shift agreement was judged after seeing the comparison, with the reliable range set after the fact. Registration: nothing was stated as fixed before the data were analysed.

imports.item: Comb filter for removing periodic leveling glitches
Slepian (multitaper) spectral estimation, NW=2, single taper

novelty_claims.quote: We present a new means for correcting tilt through a simple rotation rather than the commonly utilized spectral transfer function method
We provide a new tilt correction technique using a simple rotation to improve observations at low frequencies
We present some of the first measurements of frequency shifts from a broadband ocean bottom seismic array

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so the review sequence is not coded. The supplement (Figs S1, S2) was not supplied; the claim that the result holds at lower-tilt stations is taken from the main text. The headline is capability_characterized. Sub-claims at other statuses: (a) the OBS frequency shifts reflect real Earth structure for 14 ≤ l ≤ 37, best_explanation; (b) the deglitching is effective above 2 mHz, capability_characterized; (c) the correction gives no gain on horizontal components, reported as a failed application. The method's performance is shown in detail mainly at S17D, and the noise-floor reduction is not quantified station by station. No uncertainties are given for the tilt estimates. The peak-frequency measurement is interactive and depends on analyst judgement, so it is not fully reproducible from the text. Inference: the reliable angular-order range (14 to 37) and the attribution of the DC offset to ellipticity were set after the comparison, not before. Composition fit is imperfect: the paper is problem-led (the coverage gap), then a new capability is built and characterized, then a comparison with models follows; capability_first is the nearest fit. The S20RTS predictions were truncated at s = 12 without testing the effect of that choice.

disagreements.target: Spectral transfer-function tilt correction (Crawford and Webb 2000; Bell et al. 2015)
disagreements.support: A direct comparison at S17D and at other stations shows similar performance above 1 mHz but worse noise reduction below 1 mHz for the spectral method.
disagreements.quote: the spectral method performs worse at reducing noise at < 1 mHz, likely due to lower coherence in the lowest frequencies

disagreements.target: Glitch handling in Bécel et al. (2011)
disagreements.support: The template-subtraction deglitching removes the glitch harmonics while keeping the spectral information that Bécel et al. deleted.
disagreements.quote: One-hour harmonics were deleted in the spectra shown in Bécel et al. (2011) from the leveling glitches, effectively eliminating information

disagreements.target: Community position that asymptotic peak-shift theory is out of favor
disagreements.support: The authors argue the interactive technique is still suitable for initial quality assessment and for checking internal consistency.
disagreements.quote: asymptotic peak shift theory and associated work fell out of favor and is currently not typically pursued

disagreements.target: Noise floors in previous OBS mode studies (Bécel et al. 2011; Laske 2021)
disagreements.support: The authors attribute the earlier high noise floor below 2.75 mHz to tilt, by analogy with the noise their correction removes.
disagreements.quote: The noise floor at < 2.75 mHz is high in previous work (Bécel et al., 2011; Laske, 2021), likely due to tilt

disagreements.support: The measured shifts deviate from the reference increasingly with angular order, indicating structure the reference does not account for.
disagreements.quote: highlights important deviations that reflect unaccounted for Earth structure

disagreements.target: 3-D global models S20RTS (Ritsema et al. 1999) and SB4L18 (Masters et al. 2000)
disagreements.support: Averaged observations agree broadly with both models but differ significantly at 21 ≤ l ≤ 32.
disagreements.quote: The small but significant variations found between our observations and the two global models

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Spectral transfer-function tilt correction (Crawford and Webb 2000; Bell et al. 2015)
alternatives_considered.reason: Conserves energy across components and frequencies and avoids artefacts from band-limited spectral multiplication

alternatives_considered.chosen: Fitting and subtracting a glitch template (comb filter)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Deleting the hourly harmonics from the spectra (Bécel et al. 2011)
alternatives_considered.reason: Retains spectral information at the glitch frequencies
The community's normal-mode theory is based on acceleration, and ultra-low-frequency noise is suppressed
Similar to a Hanning window, which has been used successfully before

alternatives_considered.chosen: Omit modes strongly coupled to toroidal modes (0S11, 0S18, 0S19)
